column2: Rumaker invites John for baloney sandwiches; the Dunns invite themselves. There is enough for two; Rumaker, embarrassed, makes sandwiches for John and himself only. All four around the square oak table: John and Rumaker eat, Joe and Carol, cigarettes on their lips, follow every bite with their eyes. A meal quickly dispatched, given their hunger. Atmosphere: Burning embarrassment, a hunger sharpened by the mountain air Stakes: Material poverty tests hospitality and friendship

After the public reading of “Exit 3,” Wieners comes up close and whispers his admiring amazement: daring to have two men kiss on the mouth, and to read it aloud. Rumaker nods with a silly smile, surprised at his surprise. Words: “You dare to have the two men kiss like that?” — “And read it out loud?” Atmosphere: A whisper so as not to be overheard, a smile of admiration tinged with hesitation Stakes: The threshold of queer daring in literature; the seed of Wieners's poetic liberation

Rumaker writes long, confiding pages: he dreads the oral before the faculty, describes his mental panic, comes back to the definitions improvised in class and the critique of Dust and Oats, then questions Olson: does feeling interest him? Must he always meet him on the ground of thought? Words: if his life depended on answers before a judge, he swears they would hang him for silence; “Orally I speak well only in brief, fugitive flashes” Atmosphere: Anguished introspection, an almost tortured honesty, hope of being helped Stakes: The degree and Olson's esteem at stake; a confession of a felt intellectual inferiority

A few days after reading the letter, Olson comes to see him: not to worry about Shakespeare, to read him as a story; advice on inverted modesty and “vectors of force”; Rumaker, calmed, goes back to the essays Words: “Read him as story”; “be modest where you are immodest and immodest where you are modest”; “vectors of force in your writing” Atmosphere: Fatherly warmth, relief Stakes: The master-student bond tightens just as the student is leaving

The two friends drive in the black Morris Minor to the Pack Library; Rumaker laboriously takes notes from old volumes; after an hour, Dorn pulls him outside to a dimly lit bar in the poor part of town; beers, Ballantine ale, the mountain people's stories; Rumaker loses his scruples and convinces himself that they are doing exactly what Olson asked: looking and listening for themselves Words: Dorn: being here is more educational than being shut up in the old Pack Library Atmosphere: Guilty at first, then drunk on conviviality, soft smoke, lyrical voices Stakes: Obedience to the father against living education, resolved by paradox

After a big cleanup, Rumaker types on his old typewriter, door open; Olson, grinning, at his most affable, introduces the student in glowing terms; the plump, pasty bishop fixes him with small, dull eyes; Rumaker stumbles to his feet, nods, smiles foolishly; relief when they move off down the hall Words: Olson had said in class: “Christianity became irrelevant when it went after sex in the 1500s” Atmosphere: A last-resort comedy: a dying college made up for sale, an anticlerical rector playing the perfect host Stakes: The college's material survival against its dignity; Rumaker's old conflict with the Church

Jake brandishes the broken bottle in a menacing arc; Rumaker, seized by the impulse to offer his body, has no time to act; Fiore leaps up, spins him around, grabs him by his T-shirt and chinos, and kicks him so hard (at the small of his back) that he lifts off the ground and goes out into the night; footsteps on the gravel, laurel branches snapping, flight. Words: Jake threatens that if any of them bastards comes near him...; Fiore yells at him to get out of there Atmosphere: Extreme tension, every eye fixed, an unease that follows like a post-sacrificial calm Stakes: Lives in danger; the revelation of the veteran Fiore's violence

In the ashen light, the Dutch door bangs, Olson clears the mattresses in one immense stride, his soles passing over Rumaker's face; he opens every door, goes out the back, down the steps, and across the footbridge over the ravine toward the Studies Building; Wieners sleeps with his arm around Rumaker. Atmosphere: Gray hangover light, vibrating floors, Olson's panting breath, birds in the laurel Stakes: A nighttime conjugal hunt; Rumaker's anticipated shame at being seen entwined with Wieners

Olson, merry, spots the fishermen, brakes, leaps out, and thunders about trespassing; the man in the plaid shirt, red-faced and hard, refuses; an anti-Semitic insult; a punch square on the nose, glasses broken on the asphalt; Olson, stunned, repeats that they will have to pay; Rumaker runs for help and freezes; Field tries to calm things down. Words: Olson tells them to clear out, they have no right; the man says it is plain he is a Jew and they will shut his mouth for him; Olson cries out at what they have done: they have broken his glasses! Atmosphere: Rumaker's panic, the men's hard violence, afternoon sun on the asphalt Stakes: Olson's authority over his territory; Rumaker's betrayal

After Peak's, Dorn drives past the Gatehouse amid confused protests, turns onto the back road, circles and then crosses the cornfield, everyone jolted and laughing; Olson exults and calls for Wolpe; Rumaker imitates Wolpe's German accent and soprano; Olson, delighted, turns around to ask who that is. Words: Olson: they should have Wolpe with them; he would love it! Atmosphere: Hilarity, beer, a smell of celebration Stakes: A rare moment of Olson relaxed, complicity

Creeley, brought back from Peak's by Homire, stiff and acid on his chair under the windows, goes from student to student pouring out a vicious, threatening assessment of their human failings and their worthlessness as writers; to Rumaker, sneering, the jibe about bathing. Words: What's wrong with him, does Rumaker bathe too much? Atmosphere: Acid drunkenness, muffled threat Stakes: The collapse of an admired master

To cool Rumaker's ardor, Richard, with his sheepish smile, reassures him that his own endowments are modest, then tells high school locker room anecdotes and the story of a man at a bar's urinal whose anatomy, unrolled like a fire hose, left him outdone, eyes wide behind his glasses, hands describing a continuous unreeling. Words: Rumaker wouldn't like it anyway; he doesn't have much to brag about; “Unzipping his fly and taking it out and taking it out, trolling it out like a fire hose.” Atmosphere: Half-embarrassed teasing, locker-room complicity, tragicomic carnality. Stakes: A gentle refusal that nonetheless feeds Rumaker's hope.

When Rumaker looks glum, Richard clowns to cheer him up: he pushes out the false post tooth that replaces an incisor and spins it on the tip of his tongue, then, with a mischievous smile, pretends to swallow it. Atmosphere: Corny but affectionate clowning. Stakes: An ambiguous tenderness that keeps Rumaker's illusion alive.

Late at night, Rumaker sees through the pine branches the light on in the window of Richard's room: the sight sends him into a deep, refreshing sleep, with the most beautiful dreams, often of the two of them together; it is enough for him to know that Richard is painting, reading, or sleeping not far away. Atmosphere: An almost mystical serenity, sexual energy turned into contained, purifying energy; it strengthens his desire to write and finish his graduation project. Stakes: A chaste love that feeds the work as much as the illusion.

Right after the graduation ceremony, Rumaker takes down from the shelf above the door three piles of manuscripts a foot high, carries them outside to the rusty drum in front of the Stables, and sets them on fire; then he walks back up to Meadows Inn in the dark, stops on the wooden bridge to listen to the stream in the ravine, packs his bags, and leaves in the morning. Atmosphere: Sparks brighter than his clumsy words, a night without a lamp, a path known by heart, a sudden lightness of step Stakes: A ritual purification and the end of a green apprenticeship

In his spacious quarters on the new campus, the housekeeper washes, polishes, and mends; Albers, utterly pampered, nicknames her a Swabian pearl. Words: The kind of person who restores one's faith in humanity. Atmosphere: Bourgeois comfort, Swabian order.

Early in the morning, a few students come down from the top floor where their drafting room is; Anni, shy at first, sets out the idea that textiles were the first architectural ceiling; then cards are handed out, with black and white threads, and each weaves an inch-wide band Words: McNair: he still keeps the cards; Anni, once at ease, had sparkle and a twinkle Atmosphere: Morning intimacy, wool, cards, the future architects' astonishment Stakes: Anni finds her own voice as a teacher at Yale

A morning like any other: Bill brings pretzels and pastries, they have breakfast on the terrace, Albers takes out his camera and makes a series of portraits of Bill Atmosphere: Morning light, serene companionship above the town Stakes: An oasis of friendship amid the tensions of the HfG

At breakfast, Mr. Merritt tells Anni the rumor that Sawyer is leaving for the Metropolitan; she writes immediately to Josef in Ulm, then two days later a quick note playing down the rumor (a very poorly informed source), then three days later apologizes for having upset him; Josef replies curtly that the rumor seems organic to him and he hopes it remains one. Words: Josef: “The rumor about Charlie seems quite organic... I hope it remains a rumor” Atmosphere: Long-distance marital worry, corridor rumors Stakes: Albers's future at Yale depends on Sawyer

Rumaker surprises Ben masturbating in the bathroom; Ben, furious, yells at him to leave; Rumaker acknowledges that he cannot blame him. Words: “I want you out of here!” Atmosphere: Shame, anger, wounded empathy. Stakes: The end of living together, an urgent need for work and lodging.

Watson spies on the department over the wall of filing cabinets, stares at the badly dressed, long-haired clerk, and questions Connolly in a low voice; Rumaker thinks his double life has been unmasked; Watson nods and slips away. Words: Watson's sotto voce question to Connolly: who is that man? Atmosphere: A racing heart, then a slowing pulse; a comedy of invisibility. Stakes: Rumaker, a spy from the “commie/homo” Black Mountain at the heart of IBM, must stay undetected for six weeks.

A forbidden boozy lunch; the two mockers compare IBM computers to coffins. Words: “Exactly like the grimmest caskets of the dead”. Atmosphere: Subversive complicity, clandestine gaiety. Stakes: Inner resistance to conformity.

Rumaker takes Jack to Camille; empty back rows; the winter coat over their knees; Jack gropes under it, finds Rumaker's hand, and squeezes it relentlessly throughout the film; the bones of his fingers hurt long before Greta, her hair impeccable, coughs her last breath. Atmosphere: Dark, intimate, painfully comic; desire that literally grips Stakes: Jack's desire as a physical grip that smothers

Saturday afternoon, coming out of West 11th Street, he runs into Jack, who was just passing by; a charming monologue, eyes fixed on Rumaker; the unspoken message: go up to his room; Rumaker stammers an excuse (somewhere important to be) and flees down Christopher Street, relieved. Words: Jack: he just happened to be in the neighborhood; Rumaker murmurs that he has to be somewhere important Atmosphere: Silky charm against stupefaction; bitter relief in flight Stakes: Fleeing entanglement to preserve creative energy

A bitterly cold night, after work and the subway; Rumaker unrolls the manuscript from his pocket and reads, stumbling, the vapor of his breath in the air; Merrill listens with an attentive, amused smile; Herb is in Houston Atmosphere: Wind bellying the plastic over the windows, the cold glow of the rice-paper lamp, white-hot excitement (“steam coming out of my mouth”) Stakes: The first delivery of a text its author still believes perfect

From his desk, Rumaker sees her reading absorbedly between two letters; she calls him over: cheeks flushed, a worried confusion floating in her pale blue eyes, she says she has never read anything like it and declares herself “very impressed” Words: “I've never read anything like this before”; “very impressed” Atmosphere: Sisterly warmth and unease mixed Stakes: An unconscious test: will he dare show this text to his family?

Having typed and mailed “The Pipe” in February, Rumaker waits impatiently, checking every evening the mail spread out on the big table in the hall by the superintendent's wife, a round, earthy woman, almost always tipsy, in a stained bathrobe, who calls out names up the stairs on Saturdays. No letter or critique from Olson, usually so prompt (he corrected the manuscripts of his absent students like a correspondence course, so they would not lose what they had gained). Rumaker grows sad, doubts the story's worth, and tells himself that Olson is busy liquidating the college's assets, a thought that by itself gives him the blues. Mail on the big table in the lower hall; the superintendent's wife rarely climbs the stairs Consequences: Discouragement, thoughts of giving up the return to the college

Rumaker asks for the details of the Bovingdon loan (at least 6% annual interest; he would try to repay more), how much tuition he will have to pay, and how he could save enough in 3–4 weeks to live for one or two terms: he has been unable to save anything, and his savings will go for food. He missed A Doll's House in December for lack of money, will go see The Master Builder at the Phoenix Theatre, and on March 11 a friend is taking him to the Cherry Lane to see Anouilh's Thieves' Carnival; he is dying to see Lear, but mostly comedies are being staged. He also describes his state: the abominable 8% at IBM leaves him in a zombie state; he has written 3 stories, read a great deal, and tried without success to write sketches for the theater class; his imagination freezes as soon as he thinks of the stage. $100 lasts four months at BMC “if one is careful”; the Phoenix Theatre, 2nd Avenue; the Cherry Lane, March 11; typewriter: none; a zombie state after work Consequences: Doubts about whether the return is feasible

Late February 1955, hitchhiking from New York: wildflowers already out, the first grass, early daffodils along Lake Eden; spring comes early in the region. The place looks more run-down than in the fall. Creeley is still in Mallorca; Olson, cheerful and optimistic as always, tells Rumaker with a shy smile that he has dreamed about him a lot, without further explanation. Rumaker has brought new texts in his suitcase, including “Exit 3”; he considers “The Pipe” a failure for lack of news from Olson, but gratefully rediscovers the slower rhythms of Black Mountain life, while privately keeping doubts about the college's future that he dares not share. Daffodils along Lake Eden; hitchhiking from New York; a suitcase of manuscripts Consequences: Olson's writing classes resume

Every evening after IBM, the first thing: checking the mail on the big table in the hall; on Saturdays, the tipsy superintendent's wife in her stained bathrobe calls out names at the foot of the stairs; week after week, no letter from Olson; the exaltation of “The Pipe” degrades into doubt. Atmosphere: Feverish waiting, then a damp disappointment; the superintendent's wife's drinking as a backdrop Stakes: Does the master's silence amount to a condemnation of the work and the end of the Black Mountain dream?

An afternoon storm of tropical intensity catches Creeley and Rumaker in the Studies Building; the water blows in under the exposed lower level; Creeley abandons his laundry and takes Rumaker to his apartment at the back; the rain comes in through the big windows left open and around a piece of cardboard plugging a broken pane; he rescues the subscription checks ($2.50 a year) for the first four issues of the Black Mountain Review lying on the sill, dries them by waving them, repeating that they will still be good. $2.50-a-year checks; a broken pane plugged with cardboard; “temporary” wooden stairs dating from the construction of the 1940s Consequences: Rumaker's long-awaited conversation with Creeley comes down to platitudes and one piece of advice: vary the length of his sentences

On a very early spring night, a 'tick tick tick' wakes Rumaker; he discovers a tiny frog wrapped in a ball of dust and sets it down in the grass; it comes back night after night, slipping flattened under the door like a letter, until it grows too big and stops its visits; he will miss them.

Rumaker reads “Exit 3” one evening in class; a favorable reaction, Olson suggesting only that he remove any mention of Christmas: we all carry emotional freight with Christmas; just leave the winter. Several sessions later, when Rumaker has nothing to read, Olson reminds him of his policy; Rumaker mentions “The Pipe,” never commented on; Olson, puzzled, asks questions, scratches his head, and sends him to fetch the story from his study. Consequences: The first reading of “The Pipe” before the class

See the previous entry; correction: Rumaker reads the story in a tense voice; no laughter where he expected laughter; Olson listens hunched over, his big balding head lowered, a Camel smoking between the fingers of his big hand, then, at the last page, an interminable silence; he slowly raises his head, red-faced, stares at Rumaker with absolute seriousness, gets up abruptly on the pretext of going to urinate, and strides down the metal stairs, his work shoes clattering. When he comes back he drops into his chair, legs apart, hands on his knees, with a broad smile: “Shall we begin?” The class discusses this single story for several hours; Olson, very animated, launches into his great counter-discursive flights linking myth, tale, fantasy, and the real: the opening is as professional as can be; Billy's vision “borders on vision”; “make it a real vision”: Billy should take off and talk to the chicken hawks, make it a real fairy tale, less literal. Joe Fiore is bothered by the violence: why a murder? It isn't logical. Mary says: “This is it. I guess Olson's glad he's got a writer.” Olson announces that the next session will be devoted entirely to “The Pipe,” an unheard-of precedent. A Camel cigarette; the cane-bottomed chair Rumaker grips; the session runs past midnight; the “opening” judged flawless Consequences: Rumaker beside himself with happiness; Olson recommends sending the story to Creeley in Spain

The next session: Olson apologizes profusely; he had dug through the pile of papers on his worktable and found, inexplicably at the bottom of the pile, Rumaker's manila envelope mailed from New York, buried under letters and manuscripts from other correspondents, being too busy keeping the school afloat (which seriously cuts into his own work). A manila envelope at the bottom of a pile of mail

Rumaker, calmer, finally hears the details: Olson does not like “in a death grip” (a cliché) or “to boot” (archaic), and insists on cutting “it was stunning” (Carp would not say that). Rumaker agonizes for days over each cut but leaves some as they are, not a total robot. Expressions targeted: “in a death grip,” “to boot,” “it was stunning”
After “The Pipe,” Olson jokingly calls him a master of American speech; Rumaker takes it with a grain of salt but hears the approval, all he wanted: to keep Charles's favorable eye on him.

The tropical storm breaks; the water blows in under the lower level; Creeley abandons his laundry and leads Rumaker up the temporary stairs to his apartment; the rain comes in through the open windows and the broken pane; he slams the windows, gathers up the checks on the sill, waves them in the air to dry them, moves them; Rumaker helps him spread them out on a dry surface; the “conversation” comes down to platitudes and one piece of advice Words: Creeley, agitated, thinks the checks will be good and that they will dry here, won't they? His advice: vary the length of his sentences; he will be fine Atmosphere: Pouring rain, wet paper, helpless agitation, Rumaker disappointed and tense, a conversation chopped into pieces Stakes: The long-awaited first meeting of master and student dissolves into the trivial; the irony of the precious Review checks

Woken by a 'tick tick tick,' Rumaker looks for a luna moth, finds a tiny frog in a ball of dust, and puts it outside; it comes back, flattened under the door like a letter; its tapping becomes a soothing sound; the visits stop when it grows bigger Atmosphere: An early spring night, an icy stream outside, darkness, a peaceful intimacy with the little creature Stakes: A gentle comedy of wild daily life at Black Mountain, contrasting later with Olson's uproar

Rumaker reads, heart pounding, no laughter in the funny places; Olson hunched over, a Camel in hand; at the end, an interminable silence; Olson raises his red face, stares at each one, rushes out to urinate, work shoes clattering on the metal stairs; Rumaker's anguish; on returning, Olson slumps down, legs apart, hands on his knees, with a broad smile: “Shall we begin?”; several hours of glowing discussion, Olson very animated: the opening is as professional as can be, Billy's vision “borders on vision”; the next session devoted entirely to the story, an unheard-of precedent Words: “Shall we begin?”; “Can't get it any better”; “Make it a real vision”; Joe Fiore: why a murder?; Mary: “This is it” Atmosphere: Deadly silence, suspended waiting, then a flood of enthusiasm past midnight Stakes: The master's consecration of the disciple, and the confession of the mislaid manuscript

Shortly after Rumaker's arrival, Olson tells him with a shy smile that he has been dreaming a lot about him, with no further detail; Rumaker, delighted, wonders what he can be in those dreams Words: “I've been dreaming a lot about you” Atmosphere: Modest intimacy, the promise of an explanation to come Stakes: The master's attachment to the disciple, sealed in silence

At an earlier festival, during a lecture on twelve-tone music, Lou Harrison, composer in residence at Black Mountain, reportedly shouted from the audience, exasperated: “Well, that isn't the way Schoenberg explained it to me!”, as reported by Carroll Williams.

After two months of teaching in March and April, Creeley leaves Black Mountain and returns to Majorca to keep publishing the Review and deal with his gravely ailing marriage. Two months of teaching Consequences: Probably his last attempt at tutoring

Betty Kaiser is now gone; her affair with Charles Olson was the apparent cause of the breakup of the Olsons' “marriage,” which Connie no doubt knew about, as she did Charles's ardent correspondence with Frances Boldereff. Consequences: The Olsons' marital breakup, tension at the party

The faculty, forced by financial distress, leases large tracts of the hilly forest to timber cutters for a meagerly prolonged survival. Consequences: A symbolic destruction of the site, felt as a betrayal of the spirits of the forest.

Richard, a painting student from Detroit, arrives in the spring of 1955, as Rumaker is preparing for graduation. The student body is smaller than ever, almost nonexistent, the school in ever deeper financial trouble. The student body at its lowest; morale deteriorating in everyone. Consequences: An encounter that dominates Rumaker's last summer.

A small colony of alumni of the Art Institute of Chicago and Cass Tech High School in Detroit had migrated to Black Mountain before Richard; Jerry Van de Wiele had drawn several of them. They all knew one another and encouraged Richard to join them, describing Black Mountain to him, in the slang of the day, as a “cool and far-out” place.

Rumaker is the only openly gay student left since John Wieners's departure; Jake has left abruptly, leaving his love life almost nil. Only two or three women students, much sought after. Consequences: An extreme romantic loneliness that sharpens Rumaker's needs.

In his letters to Frances Motz Boldereff, Olson confesses his romantic confusions about Connie and other women, and even odd speculations about homosexuality, an embryonic stage of romantic development that Rumaker recognizes as his own at 23, as Olson's at 43.

Early in the relationship, in the dining hall kitchen, Olson tells Rumaker abruptly that he cannot teach him anything because he does not love him; Rumaker, through hard work at writing, then earns his respect and a measure of the coveted affection. Consequences: Rumaker transposes this pattern onto Richard, believing he can make himself loved in the same way.

Johannes Itten leads a weeklong seminar and surprises the students with the physical exercises peculiar to his method. Albers, who despises his work, comments to Anni only that some reports on him were good and others not. A weeklong seminar; physical exercises.

In late spring 1955, Olson, delighted, learns that Wieners, back in Boston, supposedly has a girlfriend, probably one of the sex workers John romanticizes; he slaps Rumaker on the back with a big, good-natured laugh.

An impromptu party co-organized by Rumaker and Wieners (perhaps suggested by Mary Fiore, as with the old teas) to break the monotony and isolation: everyone brings his own liquor and snacks; a dozen people in all, a last attempt at community cohesion as the college falls apart. The lower half of the campus closed, the big dining hall no longer available; music (Miles Davis, Charlie Parker, Stan Getz) on a portable phonograph in a corner; liquor brought by each; liquor: County Fair Bourbon, cheap whiskey bought at the state store in Asheville on weekly or biweekly trips in Tom's new Buick Consequences: The scandal of the bottle broken by Jake

Back from New England with her daughter Kate, perhaps for a last reconciliation with Charles, Connie appears transformed: an unfamiliar cream dress, her hair loose instead of in a bun or ponytail, a glass in hand near the north staircase, far from Charles, who is holding court at the south end. She drinks a lot (the first time Rumaker has seen her drink), openly compliments Rumaker and Wieners; then John Chamberlain, separated from his fiancée Elaine, isolates himself with her, one arm against the wall above her shoulder, seducing her; Rumaker sees in Connie's eyes an unfamiliar flirtatiousness born of jealousy and alcohol. A dressy cream dress, in contrast with her usual denim skirts and Mexican blouses; Streamside has an inside staircase to the upper floor with a balustrade of solid planks Consequences: Connie and Chamberlain disappear from the party together; Charles shows nothing

After a few hours, with the Olsons and Chamberlain gone, Rumaker is drinking with Mary and Joe Fiore at the square oak table; Jake appears behind the half-closed Dutch door, his torso in a filthy T-shirt among the mountain laurels, comes in kicking the bottom of the door, legs apart, fists clenched, and launches into a hate-filled harangue about his exclusion; his eyes sweep over everyone except Rumaker. Jerry Van de Wiele tries to calm him (telling him to stop putting on an act and come have a drink); Mary Fiore invites him to join them; that exasperates him. He attacks someone verbally (Jorge Fick?); a man makes a move to shut him up; Jake grabs an empty beer bottle from the table, breaks it against the edge, and brandishes the green glass weapon in a slow, menacing arc, threatening any of them bastards who comes near him… Jake's red hair gleaming in the shadow of the mountain laurels; a filthy T-shirt, chinos, worn sneakers; a bottle broken against the edge of the table, jagged green glass; eyes going from milky blue to slate gray, lips curled back to bare his teeth Consequences: The room freezes; the man backs off; Rumaker, paralyzed, has the irrational impulse to offer his body to calm Jake (end of the passage)

Late spring 1955; Rumaker tells Olson that Wieners, back in Boston, supposedly has a girlfriend, probably a prostitute friend of John's. Olson, delighted, slaps him on the back with a big, good-natured laugh. Words: “That's just what John needs… a little poontang, eh?” Atmosphere: Sunny, complicit, macho. Stakes: Olson's cheerful incomprehension of the truth about Wieners.

Rumaker is reading alone; Jake plants himself in the doorway, offers himself with his eyes, slumps down across from him; Rumaker chatters about nothing, then falls silent and stares at him; Jake looks away, his smile wavering, an icy fury in his gaze; he gets up and leaves without a word. Words: No words: only silence and looks, sham exchanges about nothing Atmosphere: Cold, a heavy silence, a seduction refused Stakes: The breakup of Jake's only source of warmth, the trigger for his coming fury

Connie arrives in a cream dress, her hair loose, already a little drunk, glass in hand, far from Charles, who is holding court at the south end; she compliments Wieners and Rumaker at length; Chamberlain comes over, traps Connie under his raised arm against the wall, and talks to her low and intensely; she answers with an unfamiliar flirtatious look; later the two of them disappear from the party. Words: Connie tells the two organizers everything she likes about them, things she had never told them Atmosphere: An almost forced gaiety, a reckless and desperate energy, magnetic seduction Stakes: Connie's declaration of independence before Charles; jealousy beneath the surface

Jake appears behind the Dutch door, his pale torso among the laurels; he kicks in the bottom of the door, comes in legs apart, fists clenched, and harangues the gathering with hatred; Jerry Van de Wiele and Mary Fiore try to calm him, in vain; he attacks someone verbally (Jorge Fick?), a man steps forward to shut him up; Jake grabs an empty beer bottle from the Fiores' table, breaks it against the edge, and brandishes the jagged glass in a slow arc; the man backs off; the room freezes; Rumaker, paralyzed, is seized by the impulse to offer his body to calm Jake. Words: Jerry tells Jake to cut the act and come drink and have fun; Mary: yes, come join them, Jake; Jake threatens any of them bastards who comes near him… Atmosphere: Frozen terror, a shrill chant like barking against the eardrums, jazz that no longer relaxes anything Stakes: A public explosion of self-hatred and exclusion; a culminating threat; what follows (beyond the passage) will tell whether blood is shed

Schweikher's letter of May 10, 1955 (the day Albers leaves for Europe); Nalle is informed only much later; in January 1956 Provost Furniss confirms to President Griswold that Nalle will not be reappointed Consequences: Crisis in the architecture department
Josef teaches at Ulm again. Anni was planning to go to Mexico with their mutual friend Sewell Sillman, but the plan falls through because of the illness of Sewell's brother.
Josef teaches at Ulm; Anni was to go to Mexico with Sewell Sillman, but his brother's illness cancels the plan.

Josef teaches at the Hochschule für Gestaltung again during the summer; Anni was planning to go to Mexico with Sewell Sillman, canceled because Sewell's brother falls ill Consequences: An aborted trip

Albers describes in his letters the new campus (an imposing complex of buildings) and his course: twenty-six students according to the album given by the students; a class of 17 men and 3 women at the first session; Bill, according to Schnaidt, spent a week in Zurich, a week in Ulm; Albers is annoyed that Bill entrusts the color course to Nonne-Schmidt 26 students; Goldring's mail (January 22, 1955) entirely in lowercase; friends have cashmere suits made (June 16, 1955)

Through her family, Mary Fiore raises the $5,250 needed to meet Forbes's deadline; Huss coldly informs Forbes by official note that the money is deposited in escrow pending the canceled notes and the deed of trust; Forbes returns the documents with a brief note regretting this end to their association and his lack of faith in Olson compared with previous rectors. $5,250 raised; money in escrow Consequences: Foreclosure avoided; the teachers' lawsuit suspended (no liability as long as the Corporation is not dissolved or in surplus); Nell Rice goes on permanent leave in June 1955.

After both matters are settled, Nell Rice, completely alienated from the college since 1954 (finding there neither a function to justify her presence nor a way of life in keeping with hers), goes on permanent leave.

Creeley returns to Black Mountain in June 1955, when the college's financial and moral situation has deteriorated further; his own impending marital breakup haunts him. Consequences: A spiral of alcohol, pot, and obsessive monologues
The twenty-six students give Albers a scrapbook containing the list of their names Atmosphere: Gratitude, attachment Stakes: Albers's teaching crosses generations and borders

At the end of the summer, Rumaker, almost always drunk, climbs the hill and shows up unannounced, late in the evening, in Richard's upstairs room at Black Dwarf, sustained by false courage and stupid chatter; it is enough for him to be in the same room. Richard, increasingly tender and then annoyed, refuses politely and calmly. Alcohol dispelling all shyness; an obsession that grows with each refusal. Consequences: Richard becomes tense and annoyed; Rumaker knows he is unbearable.
Earlier in the summer, at the same spot in front of Meadows Inn, Tom, whose marginal androgyny had gotten him into trouble, had deliberately rammed his Buick into the front of Meadows Inn.

Bill has two sandblasted glass pictures from the late 1920s (Windows, 1929; City, 1928) and two recent Homages to the Square by Albers included in the first Documenta in Kassel. 4 works: 2 sandblasted glass pictures, 2 Homages to the Square

One August afternoon, Creeley comes to Olson's drunk and high on marijuana, weeping crocodile tears and lamenting that if the world is like this, he wants no part of it. Olson, patient and supportive until then, has had enough of Creeley's drinking and pot, which make him neglect his classes. Alcohol and marijuana Consequences: After Creeley leaves, Olson, in anger and affirmation, writes the first draft of “A Newly Discovered ‘Homeric’ Hymn,” dedicated “(for Jane Harrison, if she were alive)”

Graduations were individual ceremonies: Rumaker, the painter Jorge Fick, and the poet Ed Dorn, a class of three, are the school's last graduates. Each has an outside examiner (Franz Kline for Fick) and undergoes oral questioning by the whole faculty on any subject, related to his field or not. Rumaker's letter to Charles of June 5 confessing his fear of the oral; Duncan, Rumaker's outside examiner, is then living in Mallorca with Jess Collins. Consequences: The last degrees awarded by the college.
Tom's Buick is being repaired, making money and transportation scarce and complicating even Rumaker's liquor supply, though he drinks at every opportunity. The car in the shop; nervous outbursts.

One moonless August evening, Rumaker is drinking beer with Tom (now off crutches), Jorge, Joe, and Mary Fiore. The more he drinks, the sadder he gets, feeling distant and bored by the same conversations from the same mouths after three years. He goes out several times onto the lawn in front of the house, stares at the black sky, comes back and sits sulking and inarticulate. No one pays attention to him; a poker game starts without him (he is not good enough at cards). The whole summer of frustration knots into a ball of paralyzing feverishness; he thinks again of Wes Huss's story about a desperate man who opened his veins and knew he was alive when he saw his blood, and of the line from Marlowe that Olson used to recite in class; then a terrifying silence envelops him, an immense need to speak with no words at all, he, the apprentice writer, mute even on paper. Beer; a moonless August sky; the grassy lawn in front of the house; a poker game. Consequences: An emotional low point: a psychic self-crucifixion, thoughts of blood and sacrifice.

After a moment of crushing silence in the kitchen during a poker game, Rumaker goes out, smokes a cigarette leaning against the fender of the Fiores' Jeep station wagon, then suddenly decides to end it: he takes a new razor blade from the bathroom medicine cabinet and saws at both wrists against the vehicle's grille, in the shadow of the pines, then waits to die, torn between the wish to die and a secret hope of being saved. A steel-blue Gillette blade, avoiding the small spot of oil on the flat of the blade; three clean sawing motions on the left wrist, clumsier on the right (he is right-handed); blood staining his white cotton pants; a soft, warm night; faint light filtering from the upper floors of the house through the pines. Consequences: Discovery by Jorge, rescue, bandages, Rumaker's shame and seclusion.

Jorge, leaving the poker game early, finds Rumaker bloodied against the Jeep, shouts, and runs for the others; Tom, Mary, and Joe come running. Tom, once again the army medic he had been in Korea, takes charge, has Rumaker carried inside, washes the wounds with antiseptic, declares that no tendon has been cut, shouts at him “Why did you do it, you idiot!” (more fear than anger in his voice), decides there is no need to take him to the hospital, and puts him to bed. Jorge's heavy motorcycle boots (worn in idolatry of Marlon Brando in The Wild One; he had even bought a motorcycle, which he eventually crashed on a back road near the college); no sign of a complete faint; sickroom whispers; stinging antiseptic. Consequences: Rumaker spends the night in bed, bandaged.

Waking in the middle of the night, Rumaker feels a great dark bird with broad wings land on his chest, its talons sinking into his breastbone and wanting to carry him off or tear something out of him; terrified, in a cold sweat, he looks for the bird in the shadows, then feels for the first time the pain in his wrists and burns with shame. A room blacker than ever; bandages on his wrists beginning to sting.

Around midafternoon, Olson knocks softly at the door and calls “Michael?”; Rumaker, too ashamed, plays dead. Olson hesitates, the boards creaking under his great height, then tiptoes away. Rumaker wants to call him back, but his throat tightens: it is a failed confession to the father. Rumaker remembers that Olson had already had to deal, that spring, with another suicide attempt: an effeminate young man from the South, claiming kinship with Tennessee Williams, come to study acting, who had taken an overdose in his room at Streamside and had to be rushed to the hospital in Asheville to have his stomach pumped. Olson: great height, a balding head, owl eyes behind horn-rimmed glasses (which he compares to another bird); he climbs the steps on tiptoe.

The first evening Rumaker is up, sitting on the high step near the lobby with the big stone fireplace, talking with Tom, who is making him a light meal, a child with flat blond hair (probably Paul Buck, Helene's younger son) opens and violently slams the front door before scampering off into the dusk; half a dozen or more little black snakes with yellow collars scatter across the floorboards, most of them heading for the mouth of the fireplace. Rumaker leaps up, terrified, seeing it as an omen; Tom, annoyed, picks up the remaining snakes and throws them into the tall grass outside. Half a dozen or more black “pencil snakes” with yellow collars; cracks in the fieldstone facing; a mention of the copperheads and rattlers of the hills not far from the door.

Once the wounds are half healed, Rumaker goes to apologize to Richard, stammering, utterly abject; Richard, usually gentle, looks at him with contained anger, waspish, and asks “Why did you do it?”. Rumaker will later understand that the real question was: why did you do this to me? Rumaker feared above all that he had embarrassed Richard, or even made him feel guilty (which he perhaps secretly hoped to see on his face).

An evening of beers around the kitchen table; the more Rumaker drinks, the gloomier he gets, unable to follow the conversation; he gets up several times, crosses the lobby, stares at the black, moonless sky from the lawn, and comes back to sit sulking. No one, overwhelmed by his mood, pays attention to him; a poker game starts without him. Inside him the whole summer and the three ending years knot together; Wes Huss's story of the opened veins and the line from Marlowe heard in Olson's class run through his mind; suddenly he feels around him an enormous, terrifying silence, an immense need to speak of this void and be heard, but no words, he, the apprentice writer, mute even on paper about the central fact of his life. Words: Running through his head: “See, see, where Christ's blood streams in the firmament!” Atmosphere: August heat, beer lukewarm with boredom, isolation among friends, a ball of feverishness both familiar and paralyzing, a leaden silence. Stakes: The breaking point: the writer reduced to silence about what defines him; the shadow of suicide; the eve of his leaving the world.

In the middle of a poker game, Rumaker is seized by a terrifying silence, with no words to speak of the central fact of his life; he goes out, smokes against the Fiores' Jeep station wagon, then comes back resolved: in the bathroom he takes a blue Gillette blade from the metal dispenser, turns off the light, crosses the house again without a glance toward the kitchen, and slashes both wrists against the Jeep's grille, three clean strokes on the left, clumsier on the right. He watches the blood run onto his white pants, lulled by a strange serenity, slides down against the radiator, and waits. Jorge leaves the game, sees him, shouts, and runs to get Tom, Mary, and Joe. Words: Jorge's cry on discovering the body. Atmosphere: A soft, warm night, the shadow of the pines, faint light from the windows; a surgical calm, an odd contentment, then torpor. Stakes: The mute apprentice writer lets his blood speak for him.

A nighttime awakening: a great dark bird with broad wings lands on his chest, talons sunk into his breastbone, pulling upward; he sits up in a cold sweat, looks for the bird in the black corners, finds only the new pain in his wrists and a shame that burns his face; he waits for morning, his face turned into the pillow. Atmosphere: A room blacker than ever, sacred terror, pain and shame.

A soft “Michael?” at the door in the middle of the afternoon; Rumaker holds his breath. The boards creak under Olson's great bulk as he listens, then he tiptoes away and quietly closes the door. Rumaker would like to call him back, but his throat tightens: the disloyal son who has betrayed the father. Words: “Michael?”, twice, lower and lower. Atmosphere: A closed room, held breath, the creak of the boards. Stakes: A missed confession to the father; Olson compared to another bird, an owl behind his glasses.

Gropius officially inaugurates the campus, affirming the vital necessity of creative man for the proper functioning of a true, progressive democracy Consequences: A symbolic bond sealed with the original Bauhaus

High Man (then titled Basketball Players, 1954) appears in “Sport in Art from American Collections Assembled for an Olympic Year,” organized by the American Federation of Arts and sponsored by the new magazine Sports Illustrated. The only depiction of basketball in this encyclopedic exhibition (the NBA had existed for only six years). NBA founded six years before the exhibition

The second committee of the University Council, chaired by Osborn, publishes a report: Albers's teaching is celebrated in glowing superlatives, the architecture department violently criticized; Sawyer is singled out as a potential scapegoat. Quotations: the most brilliant teaching of art, remarkable clarity, self-discipline, and enthusiasm among the students; deep and widespread confusion in the architecture department Consequences: Sawyer's fall

Contents similar to the previous exhibition: a few sports pictures and portraits. Eleanor Ward raises the price of a drawing to $75 but lowers the top price of a painting to $600. Glowing reviews from Parker Tyler (“liveliness in passivity”), James R. Mellow (“strident color,” “bravura brushwork”), and the Herald Tribune. Drawing $75, painting at most $600

Before the fall exhibition opens, Elaine writes to Ward to break off: she praises the gallery, its atmosphere, and Ward's way of doing business, but feels she is not represented by the six minor paintings selected; Ward likes neither her big baseball painting, which she worked on for two years, nor the portrait of her brother Peter, one of her most successful paintings. Worse: Ward seems to think that Elaine paints too fast and is not ready. She concludes with her usual irony: “We can celebrate over a magnum of champaigne sometime and confuse the art world”. Six paintings selected; a baseball painting worked on for two years Consequences: The end of the relationship with the Stable.

While Bill stays on Martha's Vineyard with Joan Ward and Lisa, Elaine meets Dord Fitz, an artist, teacher, and dealer from Amarillo who has come to mount a show of his students' work in a gallery on 55th Street. On the advice of the mosaicist Jeanne Reynal, Fitz knocks at the door of an initially hostile Milton Resnick, wins him over, and goes with him to a party where he meets Elaine, Kline, Nevelson, and others. Consequences: The beginning of a long working association.

Jonathan Williams and Robert Creeley, driving from New York to Black Mountain College, stop at St. Elizabeths Hospital to hand-deliver to Ezra Pound a copy of Some Time inscribed by Louis Zukofsky (Jargon edition). Pound, sitting on the lawn surrounded by his court (Eustace Mullins, John Kasper, people from Catholic University), refuses to receive them: Dorothy Pound comes to ask who they are, and Pound tells her he does not want to see friends of Charles Olson. They leave in silence. The book inscribed by Zukofsky in Brooklyn Heights beforehand; Pound sitting on the hospital lawn Consequences: The delivery of the book aborted; a symbolic anecdote about relations between Pound and Olson

Insolvency forces the sale of the whole property. The college always struggled financially; at the end, fewer students, meager funds, scarce food, essential supplies lacking (coal for the furnace), anomie, entropy. The loyalty and enthusiasm of the remaining teachers and students held. A shortage of coal for the furnace Consequences: The closing of BMC

A falling-out over complications about the continuation of Maximus; over Olson's disagreement with the authors Williams published (Patchen, Bob Brown, Mina Loy, Buckminster Fuller, anathema to Olson); and over the dispersal of the community: without a common place, distances and divergences set in; Olson sometimes treats Williams like a servant, scorns his poetry in favor of Dorn, Wieners, LeRoi Jones, and Ed Sanders, and sees his choices as a publisher as a betrayal of the movement. Fuller anathema to Olson Consequences: A partial break, but Williams remains grateful
In the spring of 1956, Creeley goes to San Francisco, which steers the magazine's last issue toward the Beat scene. Consequences: A monumental final issue.

The man who was renting the lower campus as a boys' camp decides to buy it; other prospects for selling assets materialize as needed, creating a marginal financial base to carry on. Almost all the money from the sale was to go to the accumulated debts. Consequences: Some judge the base too marginal: institutional self-cannibalization could not last.
Wolpe leaves the community for good in early 1956, believing it has no chance of long-term survival. He also declares that he could not train professionals there.
Creeley leaves in the spring of 1956, though he is expected to return.

During the winter of 1956, Fiore openly expresses his resentment of Rice: Dan is no longer a student and is taking advantage of the lack of structure to stay; he ought to leave and test his talent in New York. Rice sees it as projection but prefers simply to leave the community. Consequences: Rice leaves; a few months later Fiore himself talks of leaving; Rice will later agree to come back as Fiore's replacement.

Olson suddenly tells Huss that he is working badly and no longer wants to teach; he wants to go on living at Black Mountain with his new wife and son; if people want to come, fine; if not, that's fine too. Consequences: One more factor in the decision to close.
